1.q:
Read the passage.

Many hospitals now employ patient navigators, staff members who guide people through complicated care. A navigator might schedule follow-up appointments, explain what a referral means, or arrange a ride to a specialist across town. Some navigators are nurses; others are community health workers who speak the languages common in the neighborhood. In studies of navigation programs for cancer patients, people paired with a navigator were more likely to finish treatment on schedule. Hospitals also report fewer missed appointments, which frees time in crowded clinics. For a patient lost in a maze of forms and offices, a navigator can be the difference between getting care and giving up on it.

Which sentence best states the main idea of the passage?
o: The health care system has grown too complicated for most patients to manage without professional help.
Hospitals should hire community health workers who speak the languages of the patients they serve.
Cancer patients who are paired with a navigator are more likely to finish their treatment on schedule.
Patient navigators steer people through complex care, helping them keep appointments and complete treatment.
1.w: The first sentence introduces patient navigators, and every later sentence shows either what they do (schedule, explain, arrange rides) or what results (finished treatment, fewer missed appointments, patients getting care). Only this option covers both the role and the results that unite the whole passage.

n.0: Too broad and not stated: the passage says some patients feel lost, not that the whole system is too complicated for most patients.
n.1: Adds a recommendation the author never makes; community health workers appear only as one type of navigator.
n.2: Too narrow: the cancer-study finding is one supporting detail offered as evidence for the main idea.

1.q:
In January, Unit 6 at Bayside Hospital installed foam hand sanitizer stations at the door of every patient room, replacing the wall-mounted gel dispensers that had hung near the nurses' station. Over the next six months, the unit's rate of hospital-acquired infections fell by about a third. The infection control nurse argues that the new stations caused the drop and wants them installed on every unit in the hospital.

Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the nurse's argument?
o: Staff on Unit 6 said that the new stations were convenient and easy to use.
The stations were placed at the door of each patient room on Unit 6.
Infection rates on similar units without the new stations did not change.
The new stations cost less to buy and refill than the old wall-mounted dispensers.
1.w: If similar units without the stations saw no change over the same months, a hospital-wide cause (such as a season or new policy) becomes less likely, which supports the stations as the cause.

n.0: Convenience suggests staff might use them, but it does not show that infections fell because of them.
n.1: This repeats a detail already given in the passage, so it adds no new support.
n.3: Cost is a reason to buy the stations, not evidence that they reduced infections.

1.q:
Read the passage.

At the Riverside Public Library, a patron can check out a cordless drill, a ukulele, or a set of cake pans as easily as a novel. The branch on Elm Street lends home blood pressure monitors for two weeks at a time, and a nurse from the county health department visits monthly to show borrowers how to use them. Families can borrow laptops and wireless hotspots, which the library added after a survey showed that one in five local households lacked home internet. A seed library near the front desk invites gardeners to take packets in spring and return seeds from their harvest in the fall. Each new collection began with a request from residents.

The main idea of the passage is implied rather than stated. Which sentence best expresses it?
o: Many households in Riverside lack the home internet access they need for school and work.
The Riverside Public Library has replaced most of its book collection with tools and equipment.
A county nurse teaches library patrons how to use home blood pressure monitors each month.
The Riverside library lends a widening range of practical items in response to residents' needs.
1.w: No single sentence states the point, so combine the paragraph's details: tools, instruments, monitors, laptops, hotspots and seeds are all practical items, and the last sentence says each collection began with a resident request. Together they show the library expanding what it lends to meet community needs.

n.0: Overstates one detail: the survey found one in five households lacked internet, and school and work are never mentioned.
n.1: Distortion: the passage says patrons can borrow these items as easily as a novel, not that books were replaced.
n.2: Too narrow: the monthly nurse visit is a single detail about one collection, not the idea that unites the paragraph.

1.q:
Teresa Ferreira has worked the night shift on the cardiac unit for eleven years, and she is meticulous about medication records. She double-checks every dose against the written order, initials each entry, and has never left a blank line on a chart. New graduates are often assigned to shadow her during their first week on the unit.

Which phrases from the passage help the reader determine the meaning of meticulous? Select all that apply.
o: double-checks every dose
has worked the night shift on the cardiac unit
for eleven years
initials each entry
New graduates are often assigned to shadow her
has never left a blank line on a chart
1.w: Meticulous means extremely careful about details. Double-checking every dose, initialing every entry and leaving no blank lines are examples of that careful attention, so they serve as example clues.

n.1: Her shift tells when she works, not how carefully she works.
n.2: Length of service shows experience; an experienced nurse is not necessarily a careful one.
n.4: New graduates shadowing her suggests she is respected, but it does not describe the quality the word names; the reason for the assignment is not stated.

1.q:
Hollis Valley Health Center began texting appointment reminders to patients in March. Before then, about one in five patients missed their scheduled visits. Over the next six months, the missed-visit rate fell to about one in eight. Staff noticed that patients who replied to the text to confirm were the least likely to miss a visit, while patients with no cell phone number on file missed visits at the same rate as before. In May, the center also added Saturday hours, which several patients said made their visits easier to keep.

Which conclusion is best supported by the passage?
o: Patients with no cell phone number on file began missing more of their visits after the reminder program started.
The Saturday hours probably did more than the text reminders to reduce missed visits.
The reminders probably contributed to the drop in missed visits, but the new Saturday hours may account for part of it.
Before March, most of the missed visits happened because patients forgot the date of their scheduled appointment.
1.w: The drop came after the reminders began, and patients who confirmed by text missed least, so the reminders likely helped. But Saturday hours were added during the same period and patients credited them, so the passage supports a shared explanation, not a single cause.

n.0: This contradicts the passage: patients with no cell number on file missed visits at the same rate as before.
n.1: Nothing ranks the two changes, and patients with no cell number, who also had Saturday hours available, missed visits as often as before, which points away from this.
n.3: The passage gives no reason for the earlier missed visits; forgetting is a plausible guess that the text does not support.

1.q:
The Clearwater City Council will vote on June 9 on a plan to place 30 bike-share stations downtown. Riders would pay $2 for a 30-minute trip or $90 for a yearly pass. Supporters, including the downtown business association, say the program would reduce traffic and bring shoppers to Main Street. Opponents, including several residents of the Elm Park neighborhood, worry that the stations would take up 60 parking spaces. A similar program in nearby Fairview has averaged 410 rides a day since it opened in 2022.

What is the primary purpose of the passage?
o: to report on a proposal and the views on both sides
to criticize residents who oppose the bike-share stations
to compare Clearwater's traffic problems with Fairview's
to persuade readers to support the bike-share plan
1.w: The passage gives the vote date, the prices and the Fairview figures, and it reports both supporters' and opponents' views without taking a side. Balanced reporting of a proposal is an informative purpose.

n.1: Opponents' concerns are presented in neutral terms, with no criticism from the author.
n.2: Fairview appears once as background; the passage says nothing about traffic problems in either city.
n.3: Supporters' arguments are reported, but so are opponents' concerns, and the author never urges a vote either way.

1.q:
Each summer, Fairbanks Public Library invites children in grades 2 through 5 to log 20 hours of reading. Last year, 340 children signed up and 210 finished. Teachers at two nearby schools compared spring and fall reading scores. Children who finished the program held steady or improved over the summer, while about half of their classmates who never signed up scored lower in the fall than they had in the spring. The library points out that enrollment is voluntary and that many families who sign up already visit the library every week.

Which conclusion is best supported by the passage?
o: Children who finished avoided the fall drop in scores seen in many classmates who did not sign up.
Weekly library visits do more to improve children's reading than the summer program does.
The reading program caused the higher fall scores of the children who finished all 20 hours.
Children who signed up but did not finish the program scored lower in the fall than in the spring.
1.w: The teachers' comparison shows finishers held steady or improved, while about half of the non-participants dropped. That pattern is stated directly in the data, so this conclusion stays inside the evidence.

n.1: The passage never measures the effect of library visits separately, so no comparison with the program can be drawn.
n.2: The library notes that families choose to enroll and many already read often, so the data show a link, not proof that the program caused the scores.
n.3: The passage reports results for finishers and for children who never signed up; it gives no scores for the 130 who started but did not finish.

1.q:
In 2021, the city of Ridgeway turned four vacant lots into community gardens and assigned each plot to a household for one growing season. Gardeners harvest an average of 40 pounds of vegetables per plot each season, and many share extra produce with neighbors. In a county survey, gardeners said they ate vegetables on an average of five days a week, up from three days a week before they joined. Many also said they now cook vegetables in a wider variety of ways than they did before joining. The program's waiting list has grown every year and now includes more than 200 households, so city officials plan to open two more gardens next spring.

Which sentence from the passage best supports the conclusion that the gardens have changed how often participants eat vegetables?
o: The program's waiting list has grown every year and now includes more than 200 households, so city officials plan to open two more gardens next spring.
Gardeners harvest an average of 40 pounds of vegetables per plot each season, and many share extra produce with neighbors.
Many also said they now cook vegetables in a wider variety of ways than they did before joining.
In a county survey, gardeners said they ate vegetables on an average of five days a week, up from three days a week before they joined.
1.w: The conclusion is about a change in how often gardeners eat vegetables. Only the survey sentence compares eating frequency before and after joining (three days a week to five), so it directly supports the claim.

n.0: Growing demand shows the program is popular; it says nothing about participants' eating habits.
n.1: This shows how much the gardens produce, not how often gardeners eat vegetables; some of the harvest is given away.
n.2: This is a before-and-after change in how gardeners prepare vegetables, not in how often they eat them.

1.q:
Last spring, the town of Linwood painted 14 miles of protected bike lanes along its busiest streets. According to the town's traffic office, bicycle trips on those streets rose from about 600 to 1,050 per weekday by October. Supporters call the lanes a triumph, but the $2.3 million price tag was far too high for a town of 40,000 people. Drivers now wait longer at four downtown intersections, and that inconvenience matters more than a few hundred extra cyclists. The council should pause the project until it studies the cost more carefully.

Which of the following statements from the passage is a fact?
o: That inconvenience matters more than a few hundred extra cyclists.
The council should pause the project until it studies the cost more carefully.
The $2.3 million price tag was far too high for a town of 40,000 people.
Bicycle trips on those streets rose to about 1,050 per weekday by October.
1.w: The ridership figure comes from the town's traffic office and can be checked against its counts, so it is a verifiable fact.

n.0: Deciding that one group's inconvenience "matters more" than another's is a value judgment that cannot be proven.
n.1: "Should" signals a recommendation, which is an opinion about what ought to happen.
n.2: The dollar amount and population are facts, but "far too high" is the writer's judgment, which makes the whole statement an opinion. A number does not make a sentence a fact.

1.q:
Read the passage.

The Harmon Dam, completed in 1962, holds back Lake Harmon, which today supplies drinking water to about 180,000 people in three counties. The 240-foot dam was built mainly to control the spring floods that had repeatedly damaged farms and towns along the Silver River. A power plant was added in 1975 and now produces enough electricity for about 12,000 homes.

Photo caption: The spillway at Harmon Dam during the record flood of April 2011, when water flowed over it for 19 days in a row.

Sidebar, Visiting the Dam: The visitor center is open from Memorial Day to Labor Day. Free tours of the power plant leave hourly from 10 a.m. to 3 p.m.

According to the passage, what was the main purpose of building the dam?
o: To create a lake that would draw summer visitors
To control spring flooding along the Silver River
To generate electricity for about 12,000 homes
To supply drinking water to three nearby counties
1.w: The passage states that the dam "was built mainly to control the spring floods" along the Silver River.

n.0: The sidebar describes visiting the dam, but the passage never gives tourism as a reason for building it.
n.2: The power plant was added in 1975, thirteen years after the dam was completed.
n.3: True but answers a different question: the lake supplies water today, but the passage names flood control as the reason for building the dam.

1.q: A bar graph shows the number of flu shots given at a campus clinic each day: Monday 42, Tuesday 35, Wednesday 58, Thursday 47, Friday 63. How many more flu shots were given on Thursday and Friday combined than on Monday and Tuesday combined?
1.w: Thursday + Friday = 47 + 63 = 110. Monday + Tuesday = 42 + 35 = 77. Difference: 110 - 77 = 33.

n.0: 58 + 63 = 121 reads Wednesday's bar in place of Thursday's, and 121 - 77 = 44.
n.1: 63 - 35 = 28 compares Friday with Tuesday only, leaving out Thursday and Monday.
n.2: 110 is the Thursday and Friday total; the question asks how many more than the Monday and Tuesday total.

1.q: Each tablet of a vitamin supplement contains 0.05 milligram of vitamin B12, and a patient takes 3 tablets a day. The dietitian's log records vitamin doses in micrograms. How many micrograms of vitamin B12 does the patient take each day?
o: 50 mcg
15 mcg
150 mcg
1.w: Daily amount = 3 × 0.05 mg = 0.15 mg. Milligrams to micrograms: multiply by 1,000, so 0.15 mg = 150 mcg.

n.0: This converts one tablet correctly (0.05 mg = 50 mcg) but does not multiply by the 3 tablets taken each day.
n.1: This multiplies by 100 instead of 1,000; 1 mg = 1,000 mcg.
n.3: This multiplies by 10,000, moving the decimal point four places instead of three.

1.q: After 65% of a bottle of hand sanitizer has been used, 210 mL remain. How many milliliters did the full bottle hold? Enter the number of milliliters.

tr.323.08: Divided 210 by 0.65; the 210 mL left is 35% of the bottle, not 65%.
tr.136.5: Found 65% of 210 instead of the whole bottle.

1.w: If 65% is used, 100% - 65% = 35% remains. 210 mL is 35% of the bottle, so the whole = 210 ÷ 0.35 = 600 mL. Check: 0.35 × 600 = 210.

1.q: A student simplifies the expression 4(2x - 3) - 3(x - 5) before evaluating it. Which expression is equivalent to 4(2x - 3) - 3(x - 5)?
1.w: Distribute: 4(2x - 3) = 8x - 12 and -3(x - 5) = -3x + 15. Combine like terms: 8x - 3x = 5x and -12 + 15 = 3, so the expression is 5x + 3.

n.0: This multiplies only the x by -3 and then subtracts 5. The -3 must multiply both terms: -3(x - 5) = -3x + 15.
n.1: This distributes the 4 to 2x but not to -3. 4(2x - 3) = 8x - 12, not 8x - 3.
n.2: This multiplies -3 by -5 to get -15. A negative times a negative is positive, so -3(x - 5) = -3x + 15.

1.q: A provider orders 0.375 gram of a medication to be given once daily. The pharmacy stocks the drug as tablets labeled in milligrams. How many milligrams of the drug does the daily order call for?
o: 375 mg
1.w: Grams to milligrams is three steps down the metric ladder, so multiply by 1,000 (move the decimal point three places right): 0.375 × 1,000 = 375 mg.

n.0: This moves the decimal point four places instead of three.
n.1: This multiplies by 100, as if 1 gram were 100 milligrams; 1 g = 1,000 mg.
n.2: This divides by 1,000. Changing grams to the smaller unit, milligrams, means multiplying by 1,000.

1.q: A school nurse finds that a supply order is 2 3/5 times the size of last month's order. Which percentage is equivalent to 2 3/5?
1.w: Convert the mixed number to a decimal: 3/5 = 0.6, so 2 3/5 = 2.6. Multiply by 100: 2.6 = 260%.

n.0: 60% is the value of 3/5 by itself; the whole number 2 (200%) was dropped.
n.1: This reads 2 3/5 as the digits 2.35 instead of converting 3/5 to 0.6.
n.3: 26% = 0.26. The decimal point in 2.6 was moved only 1 place right.

1.q: At a walk-in clinic, the number of evening appointments on Monday was 4 fewer than twice the number of morning appointments. If m is the number of morning appointments, which expression represents the number of evening appointments?
1.w: 'Twice the number of morning appointments' is 2m. '4 fewer than' that amount means subtract 4 from it: 2m - 4.

n.0: '4 fewer than' a quantity means 4 is subtracted from that quantity, so the 4 comes second; 4 - 2m reverses the order.
n.2: This swaps the numbers: the morning count is doubled (multiplied by 2), and then 4 is taken away.
n.3: This subtracts 4 before doubling, which equals 2m - 8, not 4 fewer than twice m.

1.q:
A survey of 200 nursing applicants recorded job status and preferred program.
Full-time job: Day 18, Evening 46, Total 64
Part-time job: Day 52, Evening 34, Total 86
No job: Day 38, Evening 12, Total 50
Total: Day 108, Evening 92, Total 200
Of the applicants who chose the evening program, what percent have a full-time job?
1.w: 'Of the applicants who chose the evening program' sets the denominator to the evening total, 92. Full-time and evening = 46, so 46 / 92 = 0.5 = 50%.

n.0: 46 / 200 = 23% uses the grand total as the denominator instead of the 92 evening applicants.
n.2: 92 / 200 = 46% is the share of all applicants who chose the evening program, not the full-time share within it.
n.3: 46 / 64 = 71.9% uses the full-time row total, which answers 'of those with full-time jobs, what percent chose evening'.

1.q: A double bar graph shows weekly patient visits at two urgent care clinics. Northside: Week 1 124, Week 2 138, Week 3 117, Week 4 151. Southside: Week 1 109, Week 2 146, Week 3 128, Week 4 133. Over the four weeks, how many more patients did Northside see than Southside?
1.w: Northside total = 124 + 138 + 117 + 151 = 530. Southside total = 109 + 146 + 128 + 133 = 516. Difference: 530 - 516 = 14.

n.0: 530 is Northside's four-week total, not the difference between the clinics.
n.1: 52 adds the weekly gaps (15 + 8 + 11 + 18) without noticing that Southside was higher in Weeks 2 and 3.
n.3: 151 - 133 = 18 compares Week 4 only.

1.q: A toddler inhales a small bead, and an X-ray shows it lodged in one of the main bronchi. Which bronchus is it most likely in, and why?
o: The left, because it is wider and runs more vertically than the right
The right, because it is shorter, wider and more vertical than the left
The left, because the heart pushes the trachea toward the left side
The right, because it is narrower and so traps objects more easily
1.w: The right main bronchus is shorter, wider and more vertical than the left, so it continues almost straight down from the trachea and aspirated objects usually lodge there.

n.0: This describes the right main bronchus, not the left; the left is longer, narrower and angled more horizontally around the heart.
n.2: The heart sits to the left and makes the left bronchus angle away more sharply, which makes the left side the less likely site.
n.3: Right side is correct, but the reason is wrong: the right main bronchus is wider, not narrower.

1.q: During a hematology lecture, an instructor asks the class to classify blood by level of structural organization. Which classification, with its reason, is correct?
o: Cellular level, because it consists of individual cells in plasma
Organ level, because it contains several different types of cells
Organ system level, because it circulates to every organ
Tissue level, because it is a connective tissue with a fluid matrix
1.w: Blood is a connective tissue: its cells are scattered in an extracellular matrix, and in blood that matrix is fluid plasma. A tissue sits at the tissue level of organization.

n.0: Blood is a group of cells plus matrix working together, which is a tissue. The cellular level refers to a single cell.
n.1: An organ is built from two or more tissue types. Several cell types within one tissue do not make an organ.
n.2: Blood is part of the cardiovascular system, but on its own it is one tissue, not a group of cooperating organs.

1.q: A student pours water into a glass graduated cylinder, and the surface of the water curves downward in the middle. Which technique gives the correct volume reading?
o: Read the bottom of the curve with the eye level with the water surface
Read the top edge of the curve where the water touches the glass, at eye level
Read the midpoint between the top edge and the bottom of the curve, at eye level
Read the bottom of the curve while looking down at it from slightly above
1.w: Water forms a concave meniscus in glass. The volume is read at the bottom of the meniscus, with the eye level with the surface to avoid parallax error.

n.1: The top edge is where water climbs the glass; reading there overstates the volume. Read the bottom of the meniscus.
n.2: There is no midpoint convention; a concave meniscus is read at its lowest point.
n.3: Viewing from above introduces parallax error, a systematic error that shifts every reading the same way.

1.q: Under an electron microscope, a cell shows a plasma membrane, a cell wall, ribosomes and DNA clustered in a nucleoid region, with no membrane-bound organelles. Which organism could this cell most likely come from?
o: A protozoan such as Giardia
A bacterium such as Escherichia coli
A yeast cell used to leaven bread
A leaf cell from a pea plant
1.w: A nucleoid region in place of a nucleus and the absence of membrane-bound organelles mark a prokaryotic cell. Bacteria are prokaryotes, and most have a cell wall made of peptidoglycan.

n.0: Giardia is a protozoan, a single-celled eukaryote with a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles.
n.2: Yeast is a fungus, a eukaryote. It has a cell wall (chitin) but also a membrane-bound nucleus and organelles.
n.3: A pea leaf cell has a cell wall, but as a eukaryote it has a nucleus, chloroplasts and mitochondria.

1.q: Motor commands reach some effectors through the somatic division and others through the autonomic division. Which effector receives its motor commands through the somatic division of the peripheral nervous system?
o: Sweat glands in the skin of the palm
Skeletal muscle in the thigh
Cardiac muscle of the ventricles
Smooth muscle of the bladder wall
1.w: The somatic division provides voluntary control of skeletal muscle, such as the muscles of the thigh. The autonomic division controls cardiac muscle, smooth muscle and glands.

n.0: Glands, including sweat glands, are autonomic effectors; sympathetic stimulation causes sweating.
n.2: Cardiac muscle is involuntary and receives autonomic, not somatic, motor input.
n.3: The bladder wall is smooth muscle, which is controlled by the autonomic division.

1.q: A student is labeling a diagram of the male reproductive system. Which location should she label as the site where spermatogenesis, the production of sperm, takes place?
o: Lumen of the ductus deferens
Interstitial tissue of the testis
Coiled duct of the epididymis
Seminiferous tubules of the testis
1.w: Sperm are produced in the seminiferous tubules of the testis, supported by Sertoli cells. They then move to the epididymis to mature and be stored.

n.0: The ductus deferens carries sperm from the epididymis toward the ejaculatory duct; it does not produce them.
n.1: The interstitial tissue between the tubules holds the Leydig cells, which make testosterone, not sperm.
n.2: The epididymis is where sperm mature and are stored after they are made, not where they are produced.

1.q: A student touches a hot stove. Which fibers carry the temperature information from the skin of her hand into the spinal cord, and by which route do they enter it?
o: Afferent fibers entering through the dorsal root
Afferent fibers entering through the ventral root
Efferent fibers entering through the dorsal root
Efferent fibers entering through the ventral root
1.w: Two steps: fibers that carry sensory information toward the central nervous system are afferent (sensory) fibers of the PNS, and sensory fibers enter the spinal cord through the dorsal (posterior) root, whose ganglion holds their cell bodies.

n.1: The fibers are afferent, but the ventral root carries motor fibers out of the cord; sensory fibers enter through the dorsal root.
n.2: The dorsal root is the right route, but efferent fibers carry commands away from the CNS; incoming sensory signals travel on afferent fibers.
n.3: Efferent fibers carry motor commands away from the CNS, and the ventral root is their exit route, so both parts are wrong.

1.q: After swallowing, a bolus of food travels down the esophagus toward the stomach. Which statement best describes what happens to the food while it is in the esophagus?
o: Peristalsis moves it along with no absorption
Its lining absorbs water and some simple sugars
Pepsin from its wall begins protein digestion
Bile entering its lumen starts emulsifying fat
1.w: The esophagus is a muscular tube that propels the bolus by peristalsis. It neither digests nor absorbs food; the lower esophageal sphincter at its end limits reflux from the stomach.

n.1: The esophagus does not absorb anything; most absorption happens in the small intestine.
n.2: Pepsin is formed in the stomach from pepsinogen made by chief cells, not in the esophagus.
n.3: Bile enters the duodenum through the hepatopancreatic ampulla, not the esophagus.

1.q: The airway is divided into a conducting zone and a respiratory zone. Which structure belongs to the respiratory zone?
o: Alveolar duct
Laryngopharynx
Terminal bronchiole
Segmental (tertiary) bronchus
1.w: The respiratory zone (respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts and alveoli) is where gas exchange occurs. Everything from the nose to the terminal bronchioles is conducting zone.

n.1: The laryngopharynx is part of the pharynx, high in the conducting zone and shared with food.
n.2: The terminal bronchiole is the last part of the conducting zone; gas exchange begins after it, at the respiratory bronchioles.
n.3: Segmental (tertiary) bronchi are cartilage-supported conducting airways with no gas exchange.

1.q: A lab manual tells students to record every measurement in SI base units before submitting a report. Which set of units consists of SI base units?
o: Kilogram, meter, newton
Kilogram, meter, kelvin
Gram, meter, kelvin
Kilogram, liter, degree Celsius
1.w: The SI base units include the kilogram (mass), the meter (length) and the kelvin (temperature). The kilogram, not the gram, is the base unit of mass, and the kelvin, not the degree Celsius, is the base unit of temperature.

n.0: The newton is a derived unit of force (kg x m/s²), not a base unit.
n.2: The gram is a metric unit, but the SI base unit of mass is the kilogram.
n.3: The liter is an accepted volume unit, not a base unit, and the degree Celsius is not the SI base unit of temperature (the kelvin is).

1.q: A student is labeling a diagram of the thorax. Which statement correctly compares the two lungs?
o: The left lung has three lobes; the right has two lobes and a cardiac notch
The left lung has three lobes because it is larger than the right lung
Both lungs have three lobes, but the left lobes are smaller to fit the heart
The right lung has three lobes; the left has two lobes and a cardiac notch
1.w: The right lung has 3 lobes. The left lung has 2 lobes and is smaller, with a cardiac notch where the heart sits toward the left.

n.0: The sides are reversed: the left lung has 2 lobes and carries the cardiac notch, because the heart lies toward the left.
n.1: The left lung is the smaller lung (room for the heart) and has 2 lobes.
n.2: The left lung has 2 lobes, not 3; it is smaller because of the heart, but it has fewer lobes.

1.q: A storage log lists five temperatures recorded on different scales. Place the temperatures in order from coldest to hottest, starting with the coldest.
Choose the verb that correctly completes the sentence from a nursing program's orientation letter: "Everyone on the two evening shifts ___ expected to finish the safety module by Friday."
o: were
have been
are
is
1.w: Indefinite pronouns such as everyone, everybody, each and no one are singular. The phrase "on the two evening shifts" does not change the subject, so the verb is "is."

n.0: "Were" is plural and also shifts to the past; "everyone" needs the singular present "is" for a future deadline.
n.1: "Have" is plural; the singular "everyone" would need "has been," and the plain "is expected" is the form that fits.
n.2: "Everyone" is an indefinite pronoun that is always singular, so it takes "is," even though "shifts" is plural.

1.q: A staff email announces a change in the weekend schedule. Which version of the sentence uses correct subject-verb agreement?
o: Neither the aides nor the charge nurse have been told about the change.
Neither the aides nor the charge nurse were told about the change.
Neither the charge nurse nor the aides have been told about the change.
Neither the charge nurse nor the aides has been told about the change.
1.w: With "either...or" and "neither...nor," the verb agrees with the subject closer to it. "Aides" is nearer and plural, so "have been told" is correct.

n.0: With "neither...nor," the verb agrees with the nearer subject. Here that is "charge nurse" (singular), so it must be "has been told."
n.1: The nearer subject is "charge nurse" (singular), so the verb must be "was told," not "were told."
n.3: The nearer subject is "aides" (plural), so the singular "has" does not agree; it must be "have been told."

1.q: Read the sentence: "The aide remained on the unit because it was busy, so she skipped lunch until three." Which word is a subordinating conjunction?
o: remained
until
so
because
1.w: "Because" introduces the dependent clause "because it was busy", so it is a subordinating conjunction.

n.0: "Remained" is the main verb of the independent clause, not a conjunction.
n.1: "Until" is followed only by "three" (no subject or verb), so here it is a preposition.
n.2: "So" joins two independent clauses here, so it is a coordinating conjunction.

1.q: A nurse is writing a short thank-you note to a colleague. Which sentence uses a reflexive pronoun correctly?
o: My lab partner and myself presented the case study on Monday.
Please return the signed form to Ms. Park or myself by Friday.
The residents organized the whole fundraiser theirselves this year.
Kendra reminded herself to recheck the dosage before charting it.
1.w: A reflexive pronoun is correct when its antecedent is in the same clause. "Herself" refers back to "Kendra," who did the reminding.

n.0: "Myself" cannot be part of a subject; the subjective case is needed: "My lab partner and I."
n.1: "Myself" has no antecedent in this sentence; the object of "to" needs "me": "to Ms. Park or me."
n.2: "Theirselves" is nonstandard; the reflexive form is "themselves."

1.q: A medical assistant is adding suffixes to base words that end in y while writing a patient handout. Which word applies the final-y rule correctly?
o: employer
happyness
studiing
carryed
1.w: A word ending in vowel + y keeps the y before a suffix: employ (o + y) + er = "employer". Consonant + y changes y to i, except before -ing.

n.1: Happy ends in consonant + y, so y changes to i: "happiness".
n.2: Before -ing the y is kept to avoid a double i: "studying".
n.3: Carry ends in consonant + y, so y changes to i before -ed: "carried".

1.q: Marcus has finished an outline for his essay on nurse staffing. He now writes his introduction and three body paragraphs straight through, typing a note to "check this number later" rather than stopping to verify a statistic. Which stage of the writing process is Marcus in?
o: Proofreading
Drafting
Prewriting
Revising
1.w: Drafting means turning the plan (here, the outline) into sentences and paragraphs, focusing on getting the content down rather than on perfection. Leaving a note to check a detail later is typical of drafting.

n.0: Proofreading is the final check for surface errors and typos, which comes after revising and editing, not while the paragraphs are first being written.
n.2: Prewriting (planning, generating ideas, outlining) is finished; Marcus has already completed his outline and is now writing paragraphs.
n.3: Revising improves the content and organization of a draft that already exists; Marcus is still producing his first version.

1.q: A nursing student is sorting vocabulary words by prefix. Which words contain a prefix that means "not" or "without"? Select all that apply.
o: noninvasive
dysfunction
illegible
inhale
asymptomatic
antibiotic
1.w: a- means without (asymptomatic = without symptoms), non- means not (noninvasive = not entering the body), and il- means not (illegible = not readable).

n.1: dys- means bad, difficult or painful (dysfunction = abnormal function), not "not".
n.3: In inhale, in- means into (breathe in), not "not".
n.5: anti- means against (antibiotic = against life, here bacteria), not "not".

1.q: A nursing student is proofreading a care-plan template before submitting it to her instructor. Which of the following words from the template is spelled correctly?
o: recieve
seize
beleive
wierd
1.w: "Seize" is a listed exception to "i before e except after c": it is spelled e-i even though no c comes before it. The other three words need the standard pattern or a different exception.

n.0: After c the rule gives e-i: "receive". The i-e spelling reverses it.
n.2: "Believe" follows the regular rule (i before e when not after c), so the e-i spelling is wrong.
n.3: "Weird" is an exception spelled e-i; "wierd" wrongly applies the regular i-before-e pattern.

1.q: A hospital newsletter reports on its hiring committee, which acts as one group. Which sentence follows standard US agreement for this collective noun?
o: The hiring committee have met every Tuesday to review new applications.
The hiring committee meets every Tuesday to review new applications.
The hiring committee are meeting every Tuesday to review new applications.
The hiring committee meet every Tuesday to review new applications.
1.w: Collective nouns (committee, team, staff, jury, family) take a singular verb in US English when the group acts as a single unit, so "The committee meets" is correct.

n.0: "Have met" treats the committee as plural, which is British usage; US English uses "has met" for a group acting as a unit.
n.2: "Are meeting" is plural; US English treats a collective noun acting as one body as singular: "is meeting."
n.3: "Meet" is a plural verb. In US English a collective noun acting as one unit takes a singular verb: "meets."

2.q:
Daniela is writing a research paper on how well the shingles vaccine prevents shingles in adults over 50. Her instructor requires sources that are authoritative, current, and free of conflicts of interest, and warns that papers relying on personal stories or advertising will lose points. The paper is due in three weeks and must cite at least two sources on the vaccine's results. Daniela has gathered six possible sources.

Which sources meet her instructor's requirements? Select all that apply.
o: An online forum where adults describe side effects they experienced
A 1995 encyclopedia entry describing shingles and its symptoms
The CDC's current web page on how well the shingles vaccine works
A 2023 peer-reviewed study comparing vaccinated and unvaccinated adults
A magazine interview with an actor who received the vaccine
A television commercial produced by the vaccine's manufacturer
2.w: A recent peer-reviewed study is authoritative and current, and a federal public health agency's current page is authoritative with no product to sell. Both fit the instructor's criteria.

n.0: Forum posts are personal stories, which the instructor specifically warned against.
n.1: A 1995 entry is not current and cannot address how well today's vaccine works.
n.4: An actor's experience is anecdotal and is not expert evidence.
n.5: An advertisement from the manufacturer has a financial interest in the message.

2.q:
Journal entry, week one of clinical rotations: By the end of my first twelve-hour shift, my feet weighed a thousand pounds. I had taken vital signs on eleven patients, helped turn a man who had just come out of surgery, and answered more call lights than I could count. I sat in my car in the parking garage for twenty minutes before I had the energy to drive home.

The author most likely writes that her feet "weighed a thousand pounds" in order to
o: show that she worked longer than planned.
emphasize how exhausted she felt.
compare nursing with heavy lifting work.
describe swelling caused by an injury.
2.w: The statement is hyperbole, a deliberate exaggeration. Together with sitting in the car for twenty minutes before she could drive, it emphasizes extreme tiredness.

n.0: The shift is described as twelve hours with no sign that it ran over; the phrase is about how she felt, not about the schedule.
n.2: She does turn a patient, but the phrase describes her own fatigue rather than comparing nursing to another job.
n.3: This reads the exaggeration literally; nothing in the entry describes an injury.

2.q:
MEMO: To all staff, from Cafeteria Services
Starting Monday, the cafeteria will stop selling bottled soda at the register and will offer free refills of water and unsweetened tea instead. Last year, a similar change at our north campus reduced soda sales from the building's vending machines by a small amount, and staff there reported drinking more water during their shifts. Vending machines on every floor of this building will continue to stock soda. Please send any feedback to the cafeteria office by the end of the month.

Based on the memo, which conclusion is best supported?
o: Cafeteria Services plans to remove soda from the vending machines after the feedback period ends.
The change at the north campus led staff there to buy more unsweetened tea than they had before.
Staff who want soda after Monday will still be able to buy it somewhere in the building.
Soda sales across the whole building are likely to fall sharply once the cafeteria change begins on Monday.
2.w: The memo says vending machines on every floor will continue to stock soda, so soda remains available in the building after the cafeteria stops selling it.

n.0: The memo asks for feedback but announces no plan for the vending machines; it says they will continue to stock soda.
n.1: North campus staff reported drinking more water; the memo says nothing about tea purchases there.
n.3: The north campus result points the other way: vending soda sales fell by only a small amount, so a sharp building-wide drop is not supported.

2.q:
Nurse Delgado's Corner: Breakfast is the most important meal of the day, and students who skip it are making a poor choice. Your body works hard overnight. An adult human skeleton contains 106 bones, and those bones, along with your muscles and brain, need fuel each morning. A bowl of oatmeal with fruit is a better start than a frosted donut. Our cafeteria serves free breakfast from 7:15 to 7:45 a.m. on school days, so there is no excuse to arrive hungry.

Which of the following statements from the newsletter can be checked and proven true or false?
o: There is no excuse to arrive hungry.
A bowl of oatmeal with fruit is a better start than a frosted donut.
An adult human skeleton contains 106 bones.
Breakfast is the most important meal of the day.
2.w: A bone count can be checked against an anatomy reference. The number given here is wrong (an adult skeleton has 206 bones), but an incorrect statement that can be checked is still a factual claim, not an opinion. It is simply a false fact.

n.0: Whether an excuse is acceptable is a judgment, so this is an opinion even though it follows a factual sentence about the cafeteria's hours.
n.1: "Better start" is a value judgment; people can reasonably disagree about what makes a good breakfast.
n.3: "Most important" is a ranking judgment. The phrase is a familiar saying, which makes it sound factual, but no measurement can prove one meal is the most important.

2.q:
Read the passage.

City trees do more than decorate sidewalks. On a summer afternoon, a street lined with mature trees can be several degrees cooler than a treeless block nearby, because leaves shade the pavement and release water vapor into the air. Trees also catch rainwater on their leaves and bark, slowing the runoff that floods storm drains during heavy storms. Their roots hold soil in place on slopes and along streams. Some residents complain that falling leaves clog gutters and that roots crack sidewalks, and these costs are real. Still, city planners increasingly treat trees as part of a city's infrastructure, as important as pipes and pavement.

Which detail from the passage best supports the author's point that city trees work as infrastructure?
o: City planners now rank trees alongside pipes and pavement.
Trees slow the rainwater runoff that floods storm drains.
Roots can crack the sidewalks that run beside them.
Some residents complain that falling leaves clog gutters.
2.w: Infrastructure is the system of practical structures a city depends on, such as drains and pavement. Slowing runoff that would flood storm drains is a practical job trees do for the drainage system, so it directly supports the point.

n.0: This restates the author's point itself; a supporting detail must give a reason or example, not repeat the claim.
n.2: Cracked sidewalks are another conceded cost of trees, so this detail cuts against the point.
n.3: This is a cost the author concedes, a counterpoint rather than support for the main idea.

2.q:
The Lot on Fifth Street
They paved the field where I used to run,
poured gray over clover, wall over sun.
But one old oak they could not move
still splits the sidewalk, groove by groove.
Each spring it pushes, slow and sure,
a crack, a root, a little more,
till weeds and sparrows find the seam
and green comes back like a half-remembered dream.

Which theme does the poem express?
o: Nature can slowly reclaim what people have tried to cover over.
Childhood memories fade as familiar places change over time.
The speaker regrets having moved away from the old field.
Cities should protect their oldest trees from new construction.
2.w: The poem moves from paving over the field to the oak slowly splitting the sidewalk until weeds and birds return. Its message is nature's slow return through what people built.

n.1: The poem's central movement is the oak and weeds breaking back through the pavement; its one image of memory describes the green returning, not the speaker's memories fading.
n.2: The poem never says the speaker moved away; regret about leaving is not in the text.
n.3: This is a policy recommendation; the poem describes and reflects but never argues for protecting trees.

2.q:
The Riverside Community Clinic began offering evening hours in March 2024. Since then, the clinic has stayed open until 8 p.m. on Tuesdays and Thursdays, and staff recorded 1,240 evening visits in the first year. Most of these patients wrote on their intake forms that they could not leave work during the day. The clinic hired two additional nurse practitioners to cover the late shifts, using a state grant of $310,000. The evening program is the most valuable service the clinic offers, and other clinics in the county should copy it.

Which of the following sentences from the passage is a statement of opinion?
o: Staff recorded 1,240 evening visits in the first year.
The clinic hired two additional nurse practitioners to cover the late shifts.
Most of these patients wrote on their intake forms that they could not leave work during the day.
The evening program is the most valuable service the clinic offers.
2.w: "The most valuable service" is a judgment. Another reader could weigh the clinic's services differently, and no record or measurement can prove which one is "most valuable," so the sentence is an opinion.

n.0: This is a fact. The number of visits can be checked against the clinic's visit records.
n.1: This is a fact. Hiring records and the grant documents can confirm it.
n.2: This is a fact. The word "most" here describes a count of intake forms, which can be checked; it is not a judgment.

2.q:
Read the policy.

Lab Specimen Labeling Policy
Label every specimen tube at the patient's bedside, in the patient's presence, immediately after collection. Do not label tubes ahead of time. Each label must show the patient's full name, date of birth, and the date and time of collection, plus the collector's initials. Send specimens to the lab within 30 minutes of collection unless the test request is marked ON ICE; in that case, place the tube in a cup of ice and send it within 15 minutes. Blood cultures are an exception to the 30-minute rule and may be held at room temperature for up to 2 hours.

At 10:00, Ava collects a blood sample for a test marked ON ICE. The test is not a blood culture.

Which action follows the policy?
o: Label the tube at the nurses' station, place it in ice, and send it by 10:15
Label the tube at the bedside, place it in ice, and send it by 10:15
Label the tube at the bedside and send it at room temperature by 10:30
Label the tube at the bedside, place it in ice, and send it by 12:00
2.w: Tubes are labeled at the bedside. Because the request is marked ON ICE, the "unless" clause replaces the 30-minute rule: the tube goes in ice and is sent within 15 minutes of the 10:00 collection, by 10:15.

n.0: Labeling must happen at the bedside in the patient's presence, not at the nurses' station.
n.2: Applies the general 30-minute rule and ignores the ON ICE exception.
n.3: The 2-hour hold applies to blood cultures, and this test is not one.

2.q:
Read the passage.

Before electric refrigeration, ice was a crop. Each winter, crews in New England cut frozen ponds into blocks with horse-drawn plows and saws. The blocks were stacked in insulated icehouses and packed in sawdust, which slowed melting enough for the ice to last into summer. In the early 1800s, a Boston merchant began shipping ice by sea to the Caribbean, and later the trade reached as far as India. Many early cargoes melted on the way, but better insulation cut the losses. By the middle of the century, ice that had cost nothing to grow was being sold in ports thousands of miles from the ponds where it formed. The ice trade, in short, turned a winter nuisance into a worldwide business.

Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?
o: Sawdust insulation allowed ice harvested in winter to last well into the summer months.
Harvesting and shipping natural ice grew from a local winter task into a global trade.
Electric refrigeration ended a winter ice trade that had employed many New England crews.
A Boston merchant was the first person to earn a profit by shipping ice to distant ports.
2.w: The last sentence is the topic sentence: "in short" signals a conclusion that sums up the paragraph. Every earlier detail (cutting, storing, shipping, reaching distant ports) builds toward the idea that ice became a worldwide business.

n.0: Too narrow: sawdust storage is one supporting detail about how the ice lasted.
n.2: Outside the passage: the opening mentions a time before refrigeration, but the passage never describes how the trade ended.
n.3: Distortion: the passage says the merchant began shipping ice, not that he was the first to profit, and early cargoes often melted.

2.q:
Sleep Matters, a weekly podcast produced by Lakeview Medical Center, released its 100th episode in January. Each episode runs about 30 minutes and features one guest from the hospital's staff. Dr. Ada Okafor, who has directed the hospital's sleep lab since 2015, hosts the show and gives the clearest explanations of insomnia anywhere. In the latest episode, she describes a 2022 study in which adults who kept a fixed wake-up time fell asleep faster than adults who did not.

Which portion of the passage expresses an opinion?
o: who has directed the hospital's sleep lab since 2015
adults who kept a fixed wake-up time fell asleep faster
released its 100th episode in January
gives the clearest explanations of insomnia anywhere
2.w: "The clearest explanations ... anywhere" is the writer's judgment of Dr. Okafor's teaching. Listeners could reasonably disagree, and it cannot be measured or proven, so it is an opinion tucked inside an otherwise factual sentence.

n.0: Her job title and start date can be confirmed through hospital records, so this is a fact.
n.1: This reports what a study found. Whether the study found it can be checked by reading the study, so it is presented as a fact.
n.2: The episode count and release date can be checked on the podcast feed, so this is a fact.

2.q: A clinic reports that 0.6% of its scheduled appointments last month were canceled by the clinic. Which fraction, in lowest terms, is equivalent to 0.6%?
2.w: Divide the percent by 100: 0.6% = 0.006 = 6/1,000. Divide both terms by 2: 3/500.

n.0: 3/5 = 0.6, which treats 0.6% as the decimal 0.6 (that is 60%).
n.1: 3/50 = 0.06, which is 6%. The decimal point was moved only 1 place left.
n.3: 3/5,000 = 0.0006, which is 0.06%. The decimal point was moved 3 places left instead of 2.

2.q: On a dosage calculation quiz, Marcus answered 0.64 of the items correctly. Which fraction, written in lowest terms, is equal to 0.64?
2.w: 0.64 has two decimal places, so write it over 100: 64/100. The GCF of 64 and 100 is 4, so 64/100 = 16/25.

n.0: 32/50 equals 0.64, but it is not in lowest terms; 32 and 50 still share a factor of 2.
n.1: This writes 0.64 over 10 instead of 100 (64/10 = 32/5 = 6.4).
n.2: This divides 64 by 4 but 100 by 5, so the value changes: 16/20 = 0.8.

2.q: A line graph shows a patient's temperature, in °F, recorded every 2 hours: 8 a.m. 98.8, 10 a.m. 99.6, noon 101.2, 2 p.m. 100.4, 4 p.m. 99.1, 6 p.m. 98.9. Between which two consecutive readings did the temperature change by the greatest amount?
o: 2 p.m. and 4 p.m.
8 a.m. and 10 a.m.
Noon and 2 p.m.
10 a.m. and noon
2.w: Find each change: 8 to 10 a.m. +0.8; 10 a.m. to noon +1.6; noon to 2 p.m. -0.8; 2 to 4 p.m. -1.3; 4 to 6 p.m. -0.2. The largest change, 1.6 °F, is from 10 a.m. to noon, the steepest segment of the graph.

n.0: This is the largest drop, 100.4 - 99.1 = 1.3 °F, but the rise from 10 a.m. to noon is greater.
n.1: The change here is 99.6 - 98.8 = 0.8 °F, half the change from 10 a.m. to noon.
n.2: This segment starts at the peak, but the change is only 101.2 - 100.4 = 0.8 °F.

2.q: A closed rectangular box measures 10 inches long, 6 inches wide, and 4 inches high. How many square inches of wrapping paper are needed to cover the entire outside of the box with no overlap? Enter the number of square inches.

tr.124: Added the three different faces once; each face has a matching opposite face.
tr.240: Found the volume (10 × 6 × 4) instead of the surface area.

2.q: A student checks a homework answer by evaluating the expression 3x² - 2xy + y. What is the value of the expression when x = -2 and y = 5?
2.w: Substitute and follow the order of operations. 3x² = 3 × (-2)² = 3 × 4 = 12. -2xy = -2 × (-2) × 5 = +20. y = 5. Total: 12 + 20 + 5 = 37.

n.0: This squares 3x instead of x. 3x² means 3 × x² = 3 × 4 = 12, not (3 × -2)² = 36.
n.1: This misses a sign change: -2xy = -2 × (-2) × 5 = +20, not -20.
n.2: This treats x² as -4. Squaring a negative number gives a positive: (-2)² = 4, so 3x² = 12.

2.q: A pharmacy technician has dispensed 3/8 of the tablets in a full stock bottle. Which percentage of the tablets in the bottle has been dispensed?
2.w: Divide the numerator by the denominator: 3 ÷ 8 = 0.375. Multiply by 100 (move the decimal point 2 places right): 0.375 = 37.5%.

n.1: This attaches a percent sign to the decimal 0.375 without multiplying by 100.
n.2: This moves the decimal point only 1 place right; 0.375 becomes 37.5%, not 3.75%.
n.3: This divides the denominator by the numerator (8 ÷ 3 = 2.667), which converts 8/3, not 3/8.

2.q: A rideshare driver is paid $3 for each trip plus $1.25 for every mile of the trip. Which expression gives the driver's pay, in dollars, for a single trip that is m miles long?
2.w: Total = fixed amount + rate × quantity. The fixed amount is $3 per trip and the rate is $1.25 per mile, so the pay is 1.25m + 3 dollars.

n.0: 1.25m and 3 are not like terms, so they cannot be combined; 4.25m would pay $4.25 for every mile.
n.1: This multiplies the $3 trip payment by 1.25 as well, which gives 1.25m + 3.75 instead of adding a flat $3.
n.3: This swaps the two amounts: $3 is the flat payment per trip, and $1.25 is the rate that multiplies the miles.

2.q: A hospital's indoor walking path is 750 meters long. As part of a rehabilitation plan, a patient walks 4 laps of the path each day for 5 days. How many kilometers does the patient walk in total over the 5 days?
o: 150 km
1.5 km
15 km
3 km
2.w: Total meters = 750 × 4 × 5 = 15,000 m. Meters to kilometers: divide by 1,000, so 15,000 m = 15 km.

n.0: This divides 15,000 m by 100 instead of 1,000.
n.1: This divides 15,000 m by 10,000; 1 km = 1,000 m.
n.3: This is one day's distance (750 × 4 = 3,000 m = 3 km); the plan covers 5 days.

2.q: A roll of oxygen tubing is cut into two pieces for a home-care kit. The first piece measures 1.12 meters, and the second piece measures 1,165 millimeters. How many centimeters longer is the second piece than the first?
o: 45 cm
4.5 cm
2.w: Put both lengths in the same unit first: 1.12 m = 1,120 mm. Difference = 1,165 - 1,120 = 45 mm. Since 10 mm = 1 cm, 45 mm = 4.5 cm. Check in centimeters: 116.5 cm - 112 cm = 4.5 cm.

n.0: This treats 1.12 m as 11.2 cm (116.5 - 11.2). Since 1 m = 100 cm, 1.12 m = 112 cm.
n.1: 45 is the increase in millimeters; divide by 10 to change millimeters to centimeters.
n.2: This divides the 45 mm increase by 100; there are 10 mm, not 100 mm, in 1 cm.

2.q: A pre-nursing study guide is checking definitions for each level of organization. Which statement correctly defines an organ?
o: A structure of two or more tissue types working together for a function
A group of organs that cooperate to carry out a major body function
A group of similar cells that share a common structure and function
The smallest structural unit able to carry out the processes of life
2.w: An organ is a structure made of two or more tissue types that work together to perform a specific function. The stomach, for example, contains all four basic tissue types.

n.1: This defines an organ system, the level above the organ.
n.2: This defines a tissue: similar cells that work together. An organ combines more than one tissue type.
n.3: This defines a cell, the basic unit of life at the cellular level.

2.q: A microbiology student is listing features that prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells have in common. Which feature belongs on the list?
o: Linear chromosomes wound around histones
A nuclear envelope surrounding the DNA
Ribosomes that carry out protein synthesis
Mitochondria that produce most of the ATP
2.w: Both cell types have a plasma membrane, cytoplasm, DNA and ribosomes. Prokaryotic ribosomes are smaller (70S) than eukaryotic ones (80S), but both make proteins.

n.0: Linear chromosomes packaged with histones are a eukaryotic feature. Prokaryotes usually have a single circular chromosome.
n.1: A nuclear envelope belongs to eukaryotes. Prokaryotic DNA sits in a nucleoid region with no surrounding membrane.
n.3: Mitochondria are membrane-bound organelles, which prokaryotes lack.

2.q: A gastroenterology clinic schedule groups its procedures by region of the digestive tract. Which region listed below belongs to the large intestine rather than the small intestine?
o: Cecum
Duodenum
Ileum
Jejunum
2.w: The cecum is the first part of the large intestine, and the appendix is attached to it. The duodenum, jejunum and ileum together make up the small intestine.

n.1: The duodenum is the first segment of the small intestine, where bile and pancreatic juice enter.
n.2: The ileum is the final segment of the small intestine; it joins the cecum at the ileocecal valve.
n.3: The jejunum is the middle segment of the small intestine, the main site of nutrient absorption.

2.q: An atom has 17 protons, 18 neutrons and 17 electrons. Which of these quantities identifies the atom as the element chlorine rather than some other element?
o: Its mass number of 35, the sum of its nucleons
Its 17 protons, which set its atomic number
Its 18 neutrons, which fix the mass of the isotope
Its 17 electrons, which balance the nuclear charge
2.w: The atomic number (Z) is the number of protons, and it alone defines the element and its place on the periodic table. Every chlorine atom has 17 protons; any atom with 17 protons is chlorine.

n.0: The mass number (protons + neutrons) identifies a particular isotope, not the element; chlorine-35 and chlorine-37 are both chlorine.
n.2: Neutron number varies between isotopes of the same element, so it cannot identify the element.
n.3: Electron number can change when an atom becomes an ion (Cl- has 18 electrons) without changing the element.

2.q: A student traces a meal through the alimentary canal for an anatomy quiz. Immediately after chyme passes through the pyloric sphincter, which segment of the digestive tract does it enter first?
o: Duodenum of the small intestine
Jejunum of the small intestine
Ileum of the small intestine
Cecum of the large intestine
2.w: The pyloric sphincter controls emptying of the stomach into the first part of the small intestine, the duodenum. The order is duodenum, then jejunum, then ileum, then the cecum of the large intestine.

n.1: The jejunum is the middle segment of the small intestine; chyme reaches it after the duodenum.
n.2: The ileum is the last segment of the small intestine and ends at the ileocecal valve.
n.3: The cecum is the first part of the large intestine; chyme reaches it after the whole small intestine.

2.q: A lab worksheet asks students to circle the one item that represents the organ level of organization rather than the tissue level. Which item should they circle?
o: Cartilage
The skin
The epidermis
Blood
2.w: The skin is an organ (the largest in the body): its epidermis is epithelial tissue, its dermis is connective tissue, and it also contains smooth muscle and nerves, all working together. The epidermis on its own is one tissue layer.

n.0: Cartilage is a connective tissue. It forms part of organs such as joints and the ear but is not itself an organ.
n.2: The epidermis is the stratified squamous epithelium of the skin: one tissue layer of the organ, so it belongs at the tissue level.
n.3: Blood is a connective tissue with a fluid matrix (plasma). It is a tissue, not an organ.

2.q: An 11-year-old's femur is still growing longer. In which structure are new cartilage cells produced and then replaced by bone, adding to the bone's length?
o: Endosteum lining the medullary cavity
Periosteum on the outer surface of the shaft
Epiphyseal plate between epiphysis and diaphysis
Articular cartilage covering the end of the bone
2.w: Growth in length happens at the epiphyseal (growth) plate, a disc of hyaline cartilage between the epiphysis and diaphysis. Its cartilage cells multiply and are replaced by bone; after puberty the plate ossifies into the epiphyseal line.

n.0: The endosteum lines the medullary cavity and takes part in remodeling; it does not lengthen the bone.
n.1: The periosteum adds bone to the outer surface, so it increases diameter (appositional growth), not length.
n.3: Articular cartilage covers the joint surface to reduce friction; it is not the site of lengthwise growth.

2.q: A slide shows cells with a rigid outer boundary, a large central vacuole and green, disk-shaped organelles. Which other structure would these cells also be expected to contain?
o: A nucleoid region instead of a nucleus
A cell wall made of peptidoglycan
Centrioles that organize the spindle
Mitochondria for cellular respiration
2.w: The wall, central vacuole and chloroplasts identify a plant cell. Plant cells carry out cellular respiration in mitochondria as well as photosynthesis in chloroplasts.

n.0: A nucleoid region is a prokaryotic feature. Plant cells are eukaryotic and have a membrane-bound nucleus.
n.1: Peptidoglycan walls belong to bacteria. A plant cell wall is made of cellulose.
n.2: Centrioles are typical of animal cells. Most plant cells organize their spindle without centrioles.

2.q: Under a microscope, a cross section of compact bone shows concentric rings of calcified matrix surrounding a central canal that carries blood vessels and nerves. What is this structural unit called?
o: Perforating (Volkmann's) canal
Trabecula
Lacuna
Osteon (Haversian system)
2.w: Compact bone is built from osteons (Haversian systems): concentric lamellae of matrix arranged around a central (Haversian) canal that carries vessels and nerves, with osteocytes in lacunae between the rings.

n.0: Perforating (Volkmann's) canals run across the bone to connect neighboring central canals; they are not encircled by concentric rings.
n.1: Trabeculae are the thin plates and struts of spongy bone; spongy bone has no osteons or central canals.
n.2: A lacuna is the small cavity that holds one osteocyte, not the whole unit of rings around a canal.

2.q: A textbook diagram shades the parts of the nervous system that integrate and process information, separating them from the nerves that carry signals in and out. Which structures are shaded?
o: The brain, spinal cord and sensory ganglia
The spinal cord and the 31 pairs of spinal nerves
The brain and the 12 pairs of cranial nerves
The brain and the spinal cord
2.w: The central nervous system, which integrates and processes information, is made up of the brain and the spinal cord. Cranial nerves, spinal nerves and ganglia all belong to the peripheral nervous system.

n.0: Ganglia are clusters of neuron cell bodies outside the CNS, so they are part of the PNS.
n.1: The spinal cord is part of the CNS, but the 31 pairs of spinal nerves that leave it belong to the PNS.
n.2: The 12 pairs of cranial nerves are part of the PNS; they carry signals to and from the brain rather than integrating them.

2.q: A sodium atom, atomic number 11, loses one electron during a reaction with chlorine and becomes the ion Na⁺. How many protons and electrons does the Na⁺ ion contain?
o: 11 protons and 12 electrons
10 protons and 10 electrons
10 protons and 11 electrons
11 protons and 10 electrons
2.w: Protons do not change in a chemical reaction, so Na⁺ keeps 11 protons. A neutral sodium atom has 11 electrons; losing one leaves 10. Eleven positive charges and ten negative charges give a net charge of +1.

n.0: Twelve electrons would give a charge of 1-. A cation forms by losing electrons, not gaining them.
n.1: This removes a proton along with the electron. Protons stay fixed, and 10 protons with 10 electrons would be a neutral neon atom.
n.2: Ions differ from atoms in their electrons, not their protons; 10 protons would make the particle neon, not sodium.

2.q: Place these events of meiosis in the order they occur during the formation of sperm cells, starting with the first.
o: Homologous pairs line up at the cell's equator.
Homologous chromosomes separate to opposite poles.
Single chromosomes line up at the equator of each new cell.
Sister chromatids separate to opposite poles.
Homologous chromosomes pair up and cross over.
2.w: Meiosis I: prophase I (synapsis and crossing over), metaphase I (homologous pairs line up), anaphase I (homologs separate). Meiosis II: metaphase II (chromosomes line up singly), anaphase II (sister chromatids separate), giving four haploid cells.

2.q: Read the paragraph from a nutrition handout. (1) Dietary fiber offers several benefits for digestion. (2) It adds bulk to stool, which helps prevent constipation. (3) Many breakfast cereals come in colorful boxes designed to appeal to children. (4) Fiber also feeds helpful bacteria in the large intestine. (5) White bread usually costs less than whole-wheat bread at the store. (6) Foods such as beans, oats and berries are good sources of fiber. Which sentences should be removed to improve the paragraph's unity? Select all that apply.
o: Sentence 3
Sentence 5
Sentence 2
Sentence 6
Sentence 4
2.w: Sentence 3 (cereal box design) and sentence 5 (bread prices) mention foods but say nothing about fiber's digestive benefits or sources, so both break unity.

n.2: Sentence 2 gives a digestive benefit of fiber, which directly supports the topic sentence.
n.3: Sentence 6 tells readers where to find fiber, which supports the paragraph's purpose.
n.4: Sentence 4 gives a second digestive benefit of fiber, so it belongs.

2.q: Jasmine must write a report on hand hygiene in hospitals. Before writing any sentences, she sets a timer for ten minutes and writes nonstop about the topic, without pausing to fix spelling or organize her thoughts. Which prewriting technique is she using?
o: Outlining
Questioning
Clustering
Freewriting
2.w: Freewriting means writing continuously for a set time without stopping to correct or organize. It is a prewriting technique for generating ideas before drafting.

n.0: Outlining organizes ideas into a hierarchy of main points and subpoints; Jasmine is deliberately not organizing.
n.1: Questioning generates ideas by asking who, what, when, where, why and how; Jasmine is writing nonstop, not answering a set of questions.
n.2: Clustering (mind mapping) places a central idea on the page and links related ideas to it in circles and lines; Jasmine is writing continuous sentences instead.

2.q: A clinic manager is checking words formed by adding a suffix to a base word that ends in silent e. Which word is spelled correctly?
o: noticeable
desireable
arguement
truely
2.w: Silent e is normally dropped before a vowel suffix, but it is kept after a soft c or g before -able or -ous so the c stays soft: notice + able = "noticeable".

n.1: Desire ends in silent e and -able begins with a vowel, so the e is dropped: "desirable".
n.2: "Argument" is a listed exception that drops the e even before a consonant suffix.
n.3: "Truly" is a listed exception that drops the e before -ly.

2.q: A pharmacy technician is updating a supply log and must add the past-tense ending to several verbs. Which word is spelled correctly?
o: refered
occurred
admited
controled
2.w: When a word of more than one syllable is stressed on its final syllable and ends consonant-vowel-consonant, double the final consonant before a vowel suffix: oc-CUR becomes "occurred".

n.0: re-FER is stressed on the last syllable, so the r doubles: "referred".
n.2: ad-MIT is stressed on the last syllable, so the t doubles: "admitted".
n.3: con-TROL is stressed on the last syllable, so the l doubles: "controlled".

2.q: Read the sentence from a transportation notice: "Due to the fact that the main road was closed, the shuttle arrived late to the clinic." Which revision is most concise while keeping the full meaning?
o: Due to the main road closure, the shuttle arrived late.
Because the main road was closed, the shuttle arrived late to the clinic.
The main road was closed, the shuttle arrived late to the clinic.
Since the main road was closed off, the shuttle was late in arriving to the clinic.
2.w: "Due to the fact that" is a wordy way to say "because." Replacing it keeps every detail and the correct structure.

n.0: This version drops "to the clinic," so it loses part of the original meaning.
n.2: This version is shorter but joins two independent clauses with only a comma, creating a comma splice.
n.3: This version is wordier than the original idea needs ("closed off," "was late in arriving").

2.q: Danielle is writing a scholarship essay for a nursing program. Place the stages of the writing process in the order she should complete them, starting with the first.
o: Prewriting
Editing
Publishing
Drafting
Revising
2.w: Prewriting (plan: purpose, audience, ideas, outline) comes first, then drafting (write the paragraphs), revising (improve content and organization), editing (fix grammar, punctuation and spelling, ending with a proofread) and publishing (submit the final copy). Revising comes before editing because there is no point polishing sentences that may later be cut or moved.

2.q: After rereading her draft, Priya moves her strongest example to the final body paragraph and deletes a paragraph that drifts away from her thesis. To which stage of the writing process do these changes belong?
o: Proofreading
Drafting
Editing
Revising
2.w: Revising improves content and organization: adding, rearranging, removing and replacing material. Moving an example and deleting an off-topic paragraph are big-picture changes, so they are revising.

n.0: Proofreading is the final check for typos and surface errors; it does not move or delete whole paragraphs.
n.1: Drafting produces the first version from the plan; Priya is improving a draft that already exists.
n.2: Editing fixes sentence-level correctness (grammar, usage, punctuation, spelling); Priya is changing what the essay says and how it is ordered.

2.q: Maria and Lee own one clinic together. Which sentence correctly shows their shared ownership of the clinic?
o: Maria and Lees' clinic opens at eight.
Maria's and Lee's clinic opens at eight.
Marias and Lee's clinic opens at eight.
Maria and Lee's clinic opens at eight.
2.w: For joint ownership, only the last name takes the possessive: "Maria and Lee's clinic". Separate possessives (Maria's and Lee's) signal separate ownership.

n.0: Lee is one person, so the singular possessive is "Lee's", not "Lees'".
n.1: Making both names possessive signals individual ownership, which does not fit one shared clinic.
n.2: "Marias" is a plural with no apostrophe; Maria is one person and needs no s here.

2.q: A unit manager is proofreading a supply memo before sending it to staff. Which sentence from the memo uses correct subject-verb agreement?
o: The list of discharge instructions for new parents are printed in two languages.
The cost of the new monitors for all three units were higher than the manager expected.
The box of syringes on the counter by the sinks needs to be restocked today.
The results of the newborn hearing screen is ready for the family to review now.
2.w: The subject is "box," which is singular. "Of syringes" and "on the counter by the sinks" are intervening prepositional phrases, so they do not change the verb: "The box ... needs."

n.0: The subject is "list" (singular), not "instructions" or "parents" in the prepositional phrases, so the verb must be "is printed."
n.1: The subject is "cost" (singular); "monitors" and "units" sit inside prepositional phrases, so the verb must be "was."
n.3: The subject is "results" (plural), so the verb must be "are"; "screen" is the object of the preposition "of."
